title: Roger Williams Learns the Narragansett Language
text:
Roger Williams was an English minister in the Massachusetts Bay Colony who held views the colony's leaders found dangerous. He said the state should not punish religious belief, and he argued that the king's charter could not give the colonists land that belonged to the Native peoples: it had to be fairly bought from them. In late 1635 he was banished. In January 1636, warned he might be shipped back to England, he fled south through the winter snow.

Williams had spent years trading with the Wampanoag and Narragansett peoples and had learned their language. They sheltered him through that winter. In the spring the Narragansett sachems Canonicus and Miantonomi granted him land at the head of Narragansett Bay. He named the settlement Providence and opened it to people of any religion.

In 1643 Williams published A Key into the Language of America, a phrasebook and description of Narragansett life. In it he often praised their hospitality and courtesy, and he challenged the English to see that they were not superior. He served many times as a go-between between the colonists and the Native nations.
lesson: Learn the language of the people you live among and deal with them fairly. Trust is built by understanding and honest dealing, not by claims of superiority.
source: Roger Williams, A Key into the Language of America (1643); Williams's letters
